analysis.one_liner: Bars corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid from cutting pay, benefits, or jobs.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2020 with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added conditions to federal COVID-19 bailout money. Any corporation taking federal aid — emergency Federal Reserve lending, grants, loans, or loan guarantees — would have had to keep its workforce, pay, and benefits at pre-pandemic levels, including for part-time and contract workers, and could not change existing union contracts. The rules would apply from the day the company took the money until one year after either the national emergency ended or the aid was paid back. The Securities and Exchange Commission would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid — including part-time workers, contractors, and union members — who would have kept their jobs, their pay levels, their benefits, and their collective bargaining agreements for the duration of the covered period.

how_it_helps.text: Corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid must maintain the same workforce levels and benefits that existed before the March 13, 2020 emergency declaration.
The bill protects pay for every worker — employee or contractor, full-time or part-time — at or above their pre-emergency level for the whole covered period.
Companies receiving aid cannot alter any collective bargaining agreement in place on the date of the emergency declaration.
The protections last from the day aid is received until one year after the later of the emergency's end or full repayment of the aid, and the SEC is empowered to enforce and write rules.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid, which would have had to keep full payrolls and pay as a condition of taking public money. Because the bill defines federal aid to include any grant, loan, or loan guarantee, smaller corporations receiving pandemic relief could also have been covered.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'federal aid' as any grant, loan, or loan guarantee, not just large corporate bailouts — so a smaller corporation receiving pandemic relief could have been required to maintain its entire pre-pandemic payroll and pay even if its revenue had collapsed, which could make the aid effectively unusable for some firms.

The bill puts the Securities and Exchange Commission in charge of enforcing employment and labor conditions; the SEC enforces securities law and would have needed to build rules and enforcement for workplace matters, an unusual assignment that could slow or weaken enforcement in practice.

A business whose demand fell to near zero would still have to carry its full pre-emergency payroll for up to a year after repaying aid, a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against keeping workers paid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For large corporations tapping emergency Federal Reserve lending and bailout programs — many of which laid off workers while receiving support — the bill traded public money for job and pay security, a trade with clear value for workers. The design flaws are real, though: the aid definition sweeps in smaller firms that could be crushed by a hard pay-maintenance requirement, and relying on the SEC to police payrolls is an odd fit. A narrower version limited to large recipients of emergency lending would have preserved most of the benefit with fewer side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on May 8, 2020, joined by Rep. Maxine Waters as its one cosponsor.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services — the full extent of its action history.
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that received federal COVID-19 aid came out ahead: with the bill dead, they faced no requirement to keep workers, pay, benefits, or union contracts in place as a condition of taking public money, and could restructure or cut workforces freely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that took federal COVID aid

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 8, 2020, to attach worker-protection conditions to all federal COVID-19 aid.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.role: Cosponsor (the bill's only one); chair of the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill as its sole cosponsor; her committee nonetheless took no action on it after the referral.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: The only committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and held no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended, keeping the bill off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so there is no roll-call record; its support was confined to two House Democrats — the sponsor and one cosponsor — with no recorded Republican or other opposition.

industries.industry: Large corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid (recipients of Federal Reserve emergency lending and federal loans or loan guarantees)
industries.note: The bill would have made continued jobs, pay, benefits, and union contracts a condition of taking public money, ending one year after the aid was repaid or the emergency ended. Without it, these firms could take aid and still cut payrolls; the industry's interest in avoiding the condition runs against the workers the bill would protect.

industries.industry: Small businesses receiving federal grants or loans
industries.note: The bill's definition of federal aid covers any grant, loan, or loan guarantee, so smaller corporations could have been required to maintain full pre-pandemic pay even after revenues collapsed — keeping money flowing to workers but potentially making the relief unusable for the business.
Aid-receiving corporations could not alter collective bargaining agreements in place at the start of the emergency, freezing union contracts in place while public money flowed to their employers.
